prompt: You are on a normal two-way road and want to get past a slower car travelling in the same direction as you. On which side of that car must you pass?
options: On its left
On its right
On whichever side has the most space at the time
explanation: The rule is keep left, pass right: you move out to the right of the vehicle ahead, pass at a safe distance, and return left once you are clear. Passing on its left is illegal on a normal two-way road, and 'whichever side has space' is not a rule at all — the side is fixed by law, not by convenience.

prompt: A slow truck is holding you up on a single-lane road. There is a wide surfaced shoulder to the left of the yellow line. What may you legally do?
options: Move onto the shoulder and pass the truck on its left
Stay in your lane and wait until it is safe to pass on the truck's right
Straddle the yellow line so you are half on the shoulder and half in the lane
explanation: The shoulder is not an overtaking lane — you may not drive on the shoulder or the verge to get past, so both the shoulder options are wrong. The only legal overtake here is out to the right when it is safe, then back left once you are clear of the truck.

prompt: You have pulled out to the right and are overtaking another vehicle. When may you move back into the left lane?
options: As soon as your car is alongside the other vehicle's cab
The moment your front bumper is ahead of its front bumper
Only once you are safely clear of the vehicle you have passed
explanation: You return to the left only when you are safely clear — far enough ahead that you are not cutting the other driver off. Being alongside means you are still beside the vehicle, and being a bumper ahead still puts your rear across its front, which is exactly how overtaking crashes happen.

prompt: On a two-way road, when may you drive on the right-hand half of the roadway?
options: Briefly, when it is safe, no sign forbids it, or a sign or traffic officer directs you
Whenever the left-hand side has potholes you would rather avoid
At any time after dark, when there is less oncoming traffic
explanation: Encroaching on the right half is allowed only as a short, safe exception — such as overtaking — or when a road sign or an officer sends you there. Avoiding potholes and driving at night are not exceptions; the keep-left rule applies just as strongly in the dark, when you can see oncoming traffic least well.

prompt: In which one of these situations may a driver legally pass another vehicle on its left?
options: On any road, if the vehicle ahead is driving well below the speed limit
On a two-way road, if there is a wide shoulder marked off by a yellow line
On a one-way roadway with marked traffic lanes
explanation: Passing on the left is only on the table where the roadway is one-way and split into marked lanes — there is no oncoming traffic and each lane moves independently. A slow driver does not create a right to undertake, and a yellow-line shoulder is never an overtaking lane on a two-way road.

prompt: You realise the vehicle behind you wants to pass. What does the law require you to do?
options: Move as near to the left edge of the roadway as you safely can, and do not accelerate
Hold your exact position and speed so the other driver knows what to expect
Accelerate so that you pull away and the other driver no longer needs to pass
explanation: The driver being passed has a positive duty: ease left where it is safe and keep your speed steady until they are through. Holding position ignores that duty, and accelerating is the classic mistake — it strands the overtaking driver on the wrong side of the road for longer.

prompt: You are driving on an open road when the car behind you flashes its headlights at you. What does this mean and what should you do?
options: It is an insult and you should ignore it and keep your line
It warns you that your lights are faulty, so you should stop as soon as possible
It is the legal way for that driver to say they are coming past, so ease left and keep your speed steady
explanation: A flash of headlights from behind is a recognised signal that the driver intends to overtake, so you respond by moving safely left and not speeding up. Treating it as rudeness leaves the other driver exposed on the right, and stopping for a 'faulty light' invents a message the signal does not carry.

prompt: A car is halfway through overtaking you when you notice you are now below the speed limit. What are you allowed to do?
options: Speed up to the limit, because you are entitled to use the full legal speed
Keep your speed steady until the other vehicle has completely passed you
Brake hard so the other driver can get past faster
explanation: You may not accelerate until the overtaking vehicle has passed — the speed limit is a maximum you are allowed, not something you are entitled to reclaim mid-overtake. Braking hard is also wrong: a sudden change in your speed is unpredictable and can pull the other driver into danger just as badly.

prompt: You are travelling in the right-hand lane of a freeway when a faster vehicle comes up close behind you. What must you do?
options: Move into a lane on your left so the vehicle can pass
Stay where you are, since you are already at the speed limit
Move further right onto the shoulder next to the barrier
explanation: In the freeway's right-hand lane you are required to move into a lane on your left when a vehicle behind wants to pass. Being at the limit yourself gives you no right to sit in the right lane, and there is no legal move further right — the shoulder is not a driving lane.

prompt: Before you ease left to let a following vehicle pass, what must you check first?
options: Nothing — you are required to move left immediately
Only your speedometer, to make sure you are under the limit
Your mirrors and that there is safe space on your left
explanation: The duty is to move as near to the left as you can do so safely, which means checking your mirrors and the space on your left before moving. Swerving left without looking can put you into a cyclist, a pedestrian or a broken-down vehicle, and your speedometer tells you nothing about whether that space is clear.

prompt: A road is split into two roadways by a grass median. Which roadway may you drive on?
options: Either one, as long as you stay on the left side of that roadway
The left-hand roadway, unless a sign or a traffic officer directs you onto another one
The right-hand roadway, because it is the faster one
explanation: On a divided road you are restricted to the left-hand roadway; only a road sign or a traffic officer can send you onto a different one. 'Either one' ignores that restriction completely, and there is no rule that makes a right-hand roadway a legal choice for the sake of speed.

prompt: You are on a dual carriageway and you realise you have driven past your turn-off. What is the correct thing to do?
options: Carry on to the next legal crossing or interchange and come back from there
Cross the median as soon as there is a gap in the oncoming traffic
Reverse along the left edge of the roadway until you reach the turn-off
explanation: Missing a turn costs you a few minutes, not a shortcut: you continue to the next properly built crossing or interchange and turn around there. Cutting through the median is illegal no matter how clear the road looks, and reversing on a dual carriageway puts you head-on into traffic doing full speed.

prompt: What may you do with the dividing section (the median) that separates two roadways?
options: Drive along it when the roadway is congested
Park on it while you wait for a passenger
Nothing — you may not drive on, over, across or inside it
explanation: The dividing section is completely off limits: no driving on it, over it, across it or inside it, and no stopping or parking in it either. Using it to skip traffic or as a parking spot puts you in the one strip of road that other drivers never expect a vehicle to be in.

prompt: On a divided road, what is the only lawful way to get from the left-hand roadway across to the other roadway?
options: Across the dividing section, provided both roadways are clear and you do it quickly
Through a properly built intersection — and not even there if a sign or a traffic officer forbids it
Across the dividing section, provided you switch on your hazard lights first
explanation: The crossing must happen at a proper intersection built for it, and even that can be closed to you by a sign or an officer's direction. A clear road does not make crossing the median legal, and hazard lights are a warning device, not a permission slip.

prompt: You are waiting at the end of a side street to join a busy dual carriageway. When may you enter the roadway?
options: Only when you can do it without endangering other traffic
As soon as the nearest vehicle flashes its lights at you
Whenever you have waited longer than the drivers already on the roadway
explanation: Entering a roadway is only allowed when you can do so without endangering traffic already on it — the judgement is yours and the responsibility stays with you. Another driver's flash is a courtesy that cannot make an unsafe gap safe, and time spent waiting gives you no right of way at all.

prompt: Which of these may NOT be operated on a freeway?
options: A bicycle
A light delivery vehicle
A minibus carrying passengers
explanation: Bicycles are on the banned list for freeways, along with animal-drawn vehicles, tractors, motor tricycles and quadrucycles, and small or electric motorcycles. A light delivery vehicle and a minibus are ordinary motor vehicles and are not on that list.

prompt: A rider wants to take a 50 cc scooter onto the freeway to shorten the trip. Is this allowed?
options: Yes, as long as the scooter can keep up with the traffic
No — a motorcycle of 50 cc or less may not be operated on a freeway
Yes, but only in the left-hand lane
explanation: Motorcycles of 50 cc or less, and electrically driven motorcycles, are on the list of vehicles banned from freeways, so the trip is illegal no matter how it is ridden. Keeping up with traffic and staying left are both irrelevant — the ban is on the vehicle itself, not on how you use it.

prompt: You are driving on a freeway and your passenger asks you to pull over on the shoulder so they can take a photo of the view. What must you do?
options: Stop briefly on the shoulder with your hazard lights on
Stop, but only if you keep it under two minutes
Keep driving — you may not stop on a freeway for that reason
explanation: Stopping on a freeway is only allowed where a sign or a traffic officer permits it, or when something outside your control forces you to stop — a photo is neither. Hazard lights and a short stop do not create an exception; they just make an illegal, dangerous stop more visible.

prompt: Your indicators have stopped working while you are on a freeway. May you use hand signals instead?
options: No — hand signals are not allowed on a freeway
Yes, provided you make the signal clearly and early
Yes, but only when you are changing lanes to the left
explanation: Hand signals are prohibited on a freeway, so neither a clear early signal nor a left-only signal makes them legal there. At freeway speeds an arm out of the window is both hard to see and a real risk to the driver making it.

prompt: Which one of these vehicles may legally be operated on a freeway?
options: A tractor
A motor tricycle
A motorcycle with a 400 cc engine
explanation: A 400 cc motorcycle is well above the 50 cc cut-off and is not electrically driven, so it is not on the banned list. Tractors and motor tricycles are both named on that list and may not be operated on a freeway at all.
note: Deliberately avoids the unresolved learner-on-freeway question.
